initial_request.raw_prompt: Modernize the existing e-commerce monolith for incremental evolution and improved scalability. The system must support up to 50,000 concurrent users during peak campaigns, remain highly available and responsive, run on AWS, comply with GDPR, and remain operational during the migration. No fixed monetary budget has been defined; cost efficiency should be considered.

behavior.overview: This repository is a full-stack e-commerce monolith built with a Django backend and a React frontend. It provides a complete shopping experience, including user account management, product browsing and management, order processing, payment integration, and product review functionality.

partitions.name: Backend Services (ecommerce/)
partitions.role: Serves as the server-side API and database interaction layer using Django.
partitions.functionality: Handles business logic, database models, database migrations, and RESTful API endpoints for user management, catalog handling, order processing, and payment status tracking.

partitions.name: Frontend Application (frontend/)
partitions.role: Provides the user-facing web interface and client-side state management using React.
partitions.functionality: Implements the shopping UI, including screen components for product listings, cart management, checkout flows, user authentication, profile management, and order history, communicating with the Django backend via APIs.

partitions.name: System Configuration (config/)
partitions.role: Manages the global project settings and entry points for the Django application.
partitions.functionality: Contains environment-specific configurations (base, local, production), WSGI/ASGI entry points for server deployment, and the central URL routing configuration for the backend.

partitions.name: Static Assets (staticfiles/)
partitions.role: Stores client-side resources required for rendering the admin interface and the main application.
partitions.functionality: Contains bundled CSS, JavaScript, fonts, and images, including third-party library assets like Django admin static files and REST Framework documentation assets.

context_record.business_goal: Modernize the existing e-commerce monolith so it can scale during peak traffic, remain maintainable as the business grows, and evolve incrementally without disrupting ongoing operations.

blueprint.selected_pattern: Strangler Fig migration to event-driven microservices
blueprint.rationale: The Strangler Fig pattern allows for the incremental modernization of the existing Django monolith into independent microservices. This approach mitigates risk by replacing functionality module-by-module rather than via a big-bang rewrite, ensuring high availability and business continuity during the transformation.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: This architecture transforms the monolithic e-commerce platform into a scalable ecosystem, allowing individual modules (like payments or product catalog) to be updated and scaled independently. For users, this means a more responsive and reliable shopping experience, even during peak sales events. For operations and developers, it provides agility to deploy features without affecting the entire system, while ensuring adherence to GDPR compliance through better data isolation and encryption strategies.
blueprint.technical_view: The system evolves from a monolithic Django/React application to a collection of domain-aligned microservices behind an API Gateway. Communication is handled synchronously (REST/gRPC) for user-facing interactions and asynchronously (Event Bus) for backend processing. Each service is deployed as a containerized unit on AWS, owning its database schema to ensure strict data separation. GDPR compliance is enforced via centralized identity management and PII encryption at rest and in transit. Scaling is managed via auto-scaling groups, CDNs, and robust caching.
constraints_addressed: GDPR Compliance through encryption, access control, and data isolation
High availability and responsiveness for 50,000 concurrent users
assumptions: Traffic can be incrementally routed via API Gateway.
Data migration between monolith and new services is manageable via synchronization or cutover.
The current Python/Django codebase can be decomposed into services without a complete framework rewrite.
open_risks: Consistency issues during data migration between the legacy monolith database and new microservice databases.
Operational complexity of managing multiple microservices and the event bus.

adrs.title: ADR-001: Strangler Fig Migration Pattern
adrs.context: The existing monolith is too tightly coupled to replace all at once without major disruption.
adrs.decision: Use the Strangler Fig pattern to incrementally extract services.
adrs.rationale: Minimizes risk of downtime and allows for iterative delivery of scalable services.

adrs.title: ADR-002: Domain-Driven Service Boundaries
adrs.context: Need to decouple business capabilities to improve scalability and maintainability.
adrs.decision: Use Domain-Driven Design (DDD) to define microservice boundaries based on business capabilities (Identity, Product, Order, Payment, Review).
adrs.rationale: Aligns technical boundaries with business domains, reducing coupling and improving team autonomy.
negative_consequences: Requires significant analysis of existing monolithic domains

adrs.title: ADR-003: Async Event-Driven Communication
adrs.context: Synchronous request-response is a bottleneck and creates high coupling during peak load.
adrs.decision: Adopt an asynchronous event-driven architecture for inter-service communication.
adrs.rationale: Improves fault tolerance and system scalability under high concurrency by decoupling services.
negative_consequences: Increased complexity in distributed data consistency

adrs.title: ADR-004: Database-per-Service
adrs.context: Monolithic database is a single point of failure and bottleneck.
adrs.decision: Each microservice must own its private data store (database-per-service).
adrs.rationale: Prevents coupling via database, allowing independent schema evolution and scaling.
positive_consequences: Ability to select optimal DB technology per service
negative_consequences: Requires more complex data aggregation for reporting

adrs.title: ADR-005: Security and GDPR Compliance Architecture
adrs.context: GDPR requires strict protection of customer PII and adherence to security controls.
adrs.decision: Implement PII encryption at rest and in transit; centralized identity management for access control; audit logging for data access.
adrs.rationale: Essential for meeting regulatory compliance and safeguarding customer trust.

adrs.title: ADR-006: Scaling and Availability Strategy
adrs.context: System must support 50,000 concurrent users with high availability and responsiveness.
adrs.decision: Deploy auto-scaling for compute services, use CDN for static assets, and implement robust caching (Redis) for product and session data.
adrs.rationale: Ensures responsiveness and elastic scaling under peak load conditions.

retrieved_knowledge.content:
The reviewed studies reveal several distinct approaches to monolith decomposition, each with specific advantages for e-commerce contexts.

**a. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Approaches:** Multiple studies emphasize Domain-Driven Design as a foundational approach for identifying service boundaries in e-commerce systems. Abgaz et al. [1] identify DDD as a critical component of their Monolith to Microservices Decomposition Framework (M2MDF), noting its effectiveness in creating business-aligned service boundaries. Kaloudis [6] reinforces this approach, demonstrating how DDD enables better service cohesion and reduced coupling. In e-commerce contexts, natural domain boundaries often align with business capabilities, such as customer management, product catalog, order processing, payment handling, and inventory management.

Microservices architecture has emerged as a compelling alternative, offering the promise of enhanced scalability, improved fault tolerance, and greater development agility [1]. By decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, independently deployable services, organizations can achieve better resource utilization, faster deployment cycles, and improved system resilience.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) patterns have gained particular attention in the context of microservices migration, especially for e-commerce systems where business processes are inherently event-oriented. Customer actions such as placing orders, updating profiles, or processing payments naturally translate to domain events that can drive system behavior [5]. The asynchronous nature of event-driven communication provides better decoupling between services, enhanced fault tolerance, and improved scalability compared to synchronous request-response patterns [4].

ensuring the security of microservices and their interactions is crucial in e-commerce, where sensitive customer data is often processed. Abgaz et al. [6] have also stated the importance of strong security and identity management inside a microservices ecosystem. Scalability is another challenge, as e-commerce platforms often experience fluctuating traffic loads. According to the research [4], microservices should be designed to scale horizontally to suit increased demand. Furthermore, maintaining data consistency and transactional integrity across several microservices can be difficult. To solve these problems, the findings of [1] suggest investigating event-driven systems and distributed transaction patterns.

**Solution mechanics:** Each service exclusively owns its data; persistent data is accessed only through that service's API, never by another service reaching into its tables. Implementation variants (increasing isolation): private-tables-per-service, schema-per-service, and database-server-per-service (private-tables and schema-per-service have the lowest overhead). True database-per-service means separate connection strings, credentials, and lifecycle management, so a team can migrate or upgrade its database without coordinating with others. Because a single ACID transaction can no longer span services, cross-service data operations are implemented as a series of local transactions coordinated by **Sagas**, and cross-service queries use **API Composition** (the caller/gateway joins results from multiple services) or **CQRS materialized views** (a view subscribes to services' events). The **Transactional Outbox** pattern atomically updates a service's database and publishes an event.

**b. High Load Scenarios:** Asynchronous patterns (message queues) demonstrate superior throughput and availability [4].

**c. Availability:** Event-driven architectures provide better fault tolerance and system availability under stress [4].

These findings suggest that e-commerce systems should employ hybrid approaches, using synchronous communication for real-time user interactions and asynchronous patterns for backend processing and inter-service communication.

## 2.2 Monolithic and Microservices Architectures Comparison *(printed p. 478)*

In the e-commerce landscape, choosing between microservices and traditional monolithic architectures requires careful consideration of various factors. Monolithic architectures, characterized by their single, tightly coupled codebase. However, when e-commerce systems increase in size, they frequently face scalability and maintenance issues. Microservices provide an alternative approach by decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, self-contained services [6]. This decomposition results in fine-grained services, each focusing on a specific business capability. Scalability is one of the most major advantages of microservices. E-commerce platforms often experience fluctuating traffic patterns, especially during promotions or seasonal events. Microservices enable organisations to scale individual services, ensuring that resources are deployed efficiently to manage workload properly.

# Monolith-to-Microservices-Migration im E-Commerce: Zerlegung, Event-Driven Patterns und Leistung (kuratorischer Auszug)

- **Source title:** Migrating Monolithic E-Commerce Systems to Microservices: A Systematic Review of Event-Driven Architecture Approaches (curated excerpts)
- **Author(s):** Stephen W. Bulus, Olubukola D. Adekola, Folasade Y. Ayankoya, Oluwabamise J. Adeniyi, Ayodeji G. Abiodun
- **Year:** 2025
- **Knowledge box:** 2
- **Domain:** e-commerce
- **Original PDF:** `AJSTE_O1G0V4GO.pdf`

## Introduction — relevante Absätze zur E-Commerce-Migration *(printed p. 2)*

The rapid evolution of e-commerce platforms has necessitated architectural paradigm shifts to meet increasing demands for scalability, reliability, and agility [2]. Traditional monolithic architectures, while providing simplicity in development and deployment, often become bottlenecks as e-commerce systems scale to handle millions of transactions and users [3]. The centralized nature of monolithic systems creates inherent limitations in terms of independent scaling, technology diversity, and fault isolation, making them unsuitable for modern e-commerce requirements.

With a domain-driven microservices approach, each service uses the database that fits its data characteristics. Each microservice owns its private data store. This design prevents unintentional coupling between services and supports independent updates and deployments without coordinating changes across the system.

adrs.title: ADR-003: Async Event-Driven Communication
adrs.context: Synchronous request-response is a bottleneck and creates high coupling during peak load.
adrs.decision: Adopt an asynchronous event-driven architecture for inter-service communication.
adrs.rationale: Improves fault tolerance and system scalability under high concurrency by decoupling services.
negative_consequences: Increased complexity in distributed data consistency

adrs.title: ADR-004: Database-per-Service
adrs.context: Monolithic database is a single point of failure and bottleneck.
adrs.decision: Each microservice must own its private data store (database-per-service).
adrs.rationale: Prevents coupling via database, allowing independent schema evolution and scaling.
positive_consequences: Ability to select optimal DB technology per service
negative_consequences: Requires more complex data aggregation for reporting

judgment_reasons.repo_grounding: The architectural design correctly maps the existing Django monolith structure (e.g., `ecommerce/user`, `ecommerce/product`) into domain-aligned microservices, demonstrating clear alignment with the provided repository.
judgment_reasons.flaw_detection: The design fails to address the material GDPR compliance requirement concretely, providing only a high-level mention without specifying strategies like PII encryption or access control, and lacks a defined strategy for the 50,000 concurrent user performance target.
judgment_reasons.adr_soundness: The design misses a formal ADR for the 'Scaling and Availability Strategy,' a material architectural decision. Additionally, the 'Frontend Application' component lacks a corresponding ADR justification, leaving its architectural choice undocumented.
judgment_reasons.best_practice_grounding: Traceability is incomplete; FEAT-006 (Interaction Responsiveness Optimization) is not linked to any component, and material decisions regarding scaling and availability are missing from the formal ADR trail.
judgment_reasons.refinement_readiness: The identified issues (missing ADRs for scaling, compliance, and component justification, plus traceability gaps) are specific and actionable for the Architect.
